title: People preach about Solomon’s lust almost constantly.
paragraphs: People preach about Solomon’s lust almost constantly.
Seven hundred wives. Three hundred concubines. Pagan altars. Foreign gods. Compromise.
And yes… his lust was destructive.
But Scripture reveals something even more terrifying than Solomon’s sexual weakness.
It was the fact that his downfall happened while he was wildly successful.
That is the part modern believers rarely fear enough.
Because failure usually makes people cry out to God.
Success often convinces people they no longer need Him.
The most dangerous seasons in your life will probably not be the moments when you are broken, desperate, exposed, rejected, unemployed, or abandoned.
The most dangerous moments may be the seasons where everything appears blessed.

Money increases.
Influence grows.
People applaud you.
Your name carries weight.
Doors open automatically.
Your wisdom becomes admired.
Your prayers seem “effective.”
Your reputation becomes untouchable.

And slowly…
without realizing it…
your dependence on God begins to die underneath the applause.
That was Solomon’s real danger.
Not merely lust.
Success without continued surrender.
The tragedy begins long before pagan temples appear in the narrative.
It begins in the invisible places of the heart.
In 1 Kings 3:12, God gives Solomon supernatural wisdom.
The Hebrew text says:

“לֵב חָכָם וְנָבוֹן”
(lev chakam v’nāvon)
“A wise and discerning heart.”
This was not ordinary intelligence.
The word “חָכָם” (chakam) means skillful wisdom, wisdom that produces results, mastery, insight, effectiveness.
Solomon became extraordinarily competent.
And competence can become spiritually intoxicating.

There is a terrifying difference between:
being empowered by God
and
eventually believing your power belongs to you.
At first Solomon walked humbly.
In 1 Kings 3:7, Solomon says:

“אָנֹכִי נַעַר קָטֹן”
(אָנֹכִי na‘ar qaton)
“I am but a little child.”
He knew his insufficiency.
That posture protected him.
Broken dependence protects people.
But success changes weak men faster than suffering does.
By 1 Kings 10, Solomon’s kingdom looked untouchable.
Silver became common as stones in Jerusalem.
Kings traveled across nations to hear him speak.
The Queen of Sheba was overwhelmed by his wisdom, wealth, organization, authority, and atmosphere.

Externally?
He looked like living proof of God’s favor.

Internally?
Something fatal was already growing.

Scripture says in Deuteronomy 17:16-17 that Israel’s kings were specifically warned not to multiply:
horses,
wives,
or silver and gold.
But Solomon multiplied all three.
Not accidentally.
Systematically.
And this is where modern Christianity should tremble.
Because Solomon did not fall suddenly.
He drifted gradually while remaining publicly impressive.
That is the most dangerous form of spiritual decay.
You can still sound wise while your heart grows cold.
You can still lead worship while secretly loving the world.
You can still preach sermons while losing intimacy with God.
You can still build ministries while destroying your altar.
You can still appear “anointed” while heaven quietly withdraws its nearness.
That is why success can become more dangerous than suffering.
Suffering usually exposes weakness.
Success hides it.
Ecclesiastes feels haunting when viewed through this lens.
An old king speaking from the ashes of excess.
The Hebrew phrase repeated throughout Ecclesiastes is:

“הֲבֵל הֲבָלִים”
(havel havalim)
“Vanity of vanities.”
But “vanity” is too soft in English.
“Hevel” literally means vapor, breath, smoke, mist.

Something temporary.
Unstable.
Impossible to hold onto.

Solomon had everything people chase today:
wealth,
women,
power,
architecture,
fame,
influence,
intellectual brilliance,
global recognition.
And after tasting all of it…
he called it smoke.

Imagine reaching every goal people envy…
and discovering none of it can heal the soul.
That is the scream hidden inside Ecclesiastes.
The modern world worships what Solomon warned us about.

Followers.
Status.
Luxury.
Platform.
Influence.
Visibility.
Accumulation.
But Solomon discovered something horrifying:
A man can gain everything externally while collapsing internally.
Jesus later echoes this same warning in Mark 8:36:
“What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
The Greek word for “soul” here is:

“ψυχή”
(psychē)

Not merely breath.
Not merely emotion.

It refers to the inner life itself.
The self.
The eternal being.
Christ was exposing the worst trade imaginable:
external gain in exchange for internal destruction.
That was Solomon’s story.
And many believers are repeating it right now.
Because we have confused visible blessing with divine approval.
But God never measures health the way humans do.

We measure:
numbers,
attention,
growth,
influence,
money,
virality,
recognition.

God measures:
obedience,
purity,
humility,
faithfulness,
surrender,
love,
hidden devotion.
Solomon mastered building kingdoms.
But eventually neglected guarding his heart.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Above all else, guard your heart.”
In Hebrew:

“מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ”
(mikkol mishmar netzor libbekha)
“Guard your heart more than anything guarded.”
Why?
“For from it flow the issues of life.”
The tragedy is painful.

Solomon wrote wisdom many people still quote today…
yet eventually violated much of it himself.
Knowledge alone cannot save a man.
Giftedness cannot save a man.
Wisdom alone cannot save a man.
Only continual surrender can.
That is why Jesus emphasized abiding.
In John 15:5, Christ says:

“χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν”
(chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden)
“Apart from Me you can do nothing.”

Notice He did not say:
“Apart from Me you can do little.”

He said:
nothing.
The danger of success is that it creates the illusion that this verse is no longer true.
People stop trembling before God once life starts “working.”

Prayer becomes shorter.
Repentance becomes rarer.
Conviction becomes weaker.
Compromise becomes easier.
The secret place becomes optional.

And externally…
everything still looks blessed.
That is what makes Solomon’s story terrifying.
Not just lust.
Successful drift.

Anointing without intimacy.
Wisdom without obedience.
Prosperity without holiness.
Influence without surrender.
Some of the most spiritually endangered people are not struggling publicly.
They are succeeding publicly while starving privately.
And eventually the cracks appear.
Because no amount of success can sustain a soul disconnected from God.
Maybe that is why Ecclesiastes feels so emotionally exhausted.

It sounds like a man who reached the top of earth…
and discovered earth was too small to satisfy eternity.
Only Christ can satisfy what success never will.
Only Jesus can heal what accomplishment cannot touch.
Only intimacy with God can keep success from becoming an idol.
This message is not only for leaders.
It is for anyone chasing something so aggressively that they are slowly losing the presence of God while achieving it.
Do not let your blessings become the reason you stop depending on the One who gave them.
The enemy is not always trying to destroy you through pain.
Sometimes he tries to destroy you through applause.

Be honest.
This hit some people harder than they expected.
Send this to someone building a career, platform, ministry, business, or future who desperately needs this warning before success becomes spiritual poison.

And the scariest part is this:
Solomon did not realize he was drifting until the drift had already built temples.
